title: Mixture-of-Experts Transformer
subtitle: Topic: Mixture-of-Experts Transformer · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture · 7 questions, 28 options, 7 compact diagrams and one tested PyTorch example.
hero:
MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS TRANSFORMER · TRANSFORMERS AND LLM ARCHITECTURE

Shared attention. Routed expert MLPs.

Learn how Transformer attention, token-wise expert selection, and sparse feed-forward computation fit together.

questions.stem: In a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer, which part of a standard Transformer block is typically replaced by experts, and what still happens in self-attention?
options: An MoE Transformer replaces individual self-attention heads with routed expert networks, while its feed-forward sublayers remain unchanged. The router decides which past token positions each expert may attend to during every attention calculation.

An MoE Transformer replaces feed-forward sublayers with routed experts, but those experts also normally perform all token-to-token attention calculations. Shared self-attention is removed, so routing alone determines how contextual information flows across positions.

A typical MoE Transformer replaces some feed-forward sublayers with routed expert networks. Self-attention still mixes information across token positions, while a learned router selects a small expert subset for each token's feed-forward processing.

An MoE Transformer keeps shared attention and expert feed-forward layers, but the router selects one fixed expert group for the training dataset. Every token in each transformer block follows that same expert assignment.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A Transformer block normally uses self-attention to mix information across tokens and a feed-forward network to transform each token's features. In many MoE Transformers, some feed-forward networks are replaced by several expert MLPs. A learned router decides which few experts process each token, while attention remains shared. For example, a translation model may use attention to connect a pronoun with its context, then route that token through selected feed-forward experts. MoE does not automatically replace attention itself.

questions.stem: Why can a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer have many more total parameters than a dense Transformer while using relatively few expert parameters for each token?
options: An MoE Transformer stores many expert feed-forward networks but activates only a small top-k subset for each token. Total parameter capacity grows, while active expert computation stays limited; all experts still require memory somewhere.

An MoE Transformer increases total parameters by replicating every attention layer, but runs only one attention replica per token. Expert feed-forward networks remain fully dense, so the savings come entirely from skipped attention computations.

An MoE Transformer stores many expert feed-forward networks but executes every expert for each token. The router only adjusts the weighted average afterward, so the number of active parameters equals the expert parameter count.

An MoE Transformer saves memory by unloading every expert except the selected top-k before each token arrives. Inactive expert weights need no storage, so increasing the total number of experts never raises memory demands.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A dense Transformer feed-forward layer generally uses the same parameter block for every token. In a sparse MoE Transformer, many expert blocks are stored, but each token is sent to only a few. Imagine eight experts with top-2 routing: two experts run per token, although all eight increase the model's total stored parameters. Attention and router computation also remain. This can expand capacity at a lower expert-compute cost than executing all eight experts, but memory and distributed dispatch still matter.

questions.stem: How does top-k routing choose experts for different tokens in an MoE Transformer, and how are their feed-forward outputs combined?
options: The router scores experts once for an entire prompt, selects one common top-k subset for all tokens, and merges the resulting feed-forward outputs. Individual token representations do not influence expert choices within that sequence.

The router scores available experts for every token, but sends each token through all expert feed-forward networks before selecting the best k outputs. Routing therefore changes aggregation weights without reducing the executed expert computations.

The router scores experts for each token and selects its top-k subset, but keeps only the highest-scoring expert output. Lower-ranked selected experts are recorded for statistics, never computed or included in the resulting representation.

The router scores experts separately for each token's hidden state, selects its highest-ranked k experts, and applies routing weights to their feed-forward outputs. The combined result returns to the Transformer block for residual processing.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The router takes each token's current hidden vector and scores the available experts. Top-k selection sends the token to a few experts, whose outputs are combined with routing weights. For example, two tokens in the same sentence might choose different expert pairs because their hidden states differ. The combined output becomes the feed-forward contribution of that Transformer layer and is added through its residual path. Implementations may normalize routing weights differently, so inspect the chosen architecture.

questions.stem: Why do MoE Transformers need expert load balancing during training, and how can auxiliary routing losses or capacity limits affect the results?
options: Without balancing, experts receive unequal token counts, but overloaded experts always run at the same speed as idle ones. Auxiliary routing losses improve attention accuracy only, while capacity limits cannot change token execution behavior.

Without balancing, a router may overload a few experts while others receive little training. Auxiliary losses can encourage distributed assignments, and capacity rules manage overflow, but aggressive balancing or token dropping may affect quality.

Without balancing, expert popularity can vary, so the router should send every token through every expert. Auxiliary objectives then become completely unnecessary, and capacity limits can be permanently removed without affecting sparse expert computation.

Without balancing, some experts may receive too few tokens, but capacity limits always guarantee every assignment executes without delays or dropping. Auxiliary losses enforce exactly equal usage without measurably influencing the model's learned representations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Top-k routing can concentrate tokens on a small group of experts. This creates bottlenecks and leaves other experts poorly trained. An auxiliary load-balancing loss can encourage a healthier distribution, while capacity factors can limit how much work each expert receives. For example, a chat model might overload the same GPU's experts on a particular input mix. Some implementations drop or reroute excess tokens, while dropless designs retain them at added cost. Engineers should monitor both token distribution and model quality.

questions.stem: How can a small PyTorch MoE Transformer demonstration combine shared multi-head self-attention with top-2 routed feed-forward experts and a residual connection?
options: First compute shared multi-head attention and add its residual output. Then score each token, choose two feed-forward experts, run only assigned token rows, weight and merge their outputs, and add the MoE residual.

First compute multi-head attention separately inside every expert and merge the full attention outputs. Then select two experts from their completed predictions, while the shared feed-forward block processes all tokens without sparse dispatch.

First compute shared multi-head attention and add its residual. Then score tokens using fixed, nontrainable expert preferences, execute every expert on the batch, and use top-k only to decide which outputs to display.

First compute shared multi-head attention, then choose two experts for the batch instead of individual tokens. Process that common subset and discard the attention residual, leaving the transformer representation dependent solely on experts.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A minimal MoE Transformer block keeps one shared multi-head attention layer and replaces the standard feed-forward part with expert MLPs. The code below flattens token hidden states, scores four experts, selects two per token, dispatches selected rows, and combines their outputs with normalized scores. It adds attention and expert residuals, then backpropagates a sample loss. For example, a toy language-model block can demonstrate the computation on CPU. Production Transformers additionally use layer normalization, optimized kernels, masks, and scalable dispatch.

questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

A tiny MoE Transformer in PyTorch

PyTorch · attention + top-2 expert MLPs 15 lines
01 import torch
02 from torch import nn
03 x = torch.randn(2, 3, 8, requires_grad=True)
04 attn, gate = nn.MultiheadAttention(8, 2, batch_first=True), nn.Linear(8, 4)
05 experts = nn.ModuleList(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(8,16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16,8)) for _ in range(4))
06 h = x + attn(x, x, x, need_weights=False)[0]
07 flat = h.reshape(-1, 8)
08 scores, ids = gate(flat).softmax(-1).topk(2, dim=-1)
09 scores = scores / scores.sum(-1, keepdim=True)
10 out = torch.zeros_like(flat)
11 for eid, expert in enumerate(experts):
12     token, slot = (ids == eid).nonzero(as_tuple=True)
13     if token.numel(): out.index_add_(0, token, scores[token,slot,None] * expert(flat[token]))
14 loss = (h + out.reshape_as(h)).square().mean(); loss.backward()
15 print(h.shape, gate.weight.grad is not None)

Executable CPU demonstration (PyTorch). It omits masks, layer normalization, balancing, and distributed dispatch; it does backpropagate router gradients.

Shared attention feeds a top-2 expert block; the result joins a residual connection.

questions.stem: During autoregressive generation with an MoE Transformer, how do the attention KV cache and expert routing differ, and what can still cause inference latency spikes?
options: The KV cache stores every expert's output for reuse on future tokens, so routing happens only during the first decoding step. Latency spikes therefore come solely from attention-score calculations, not expert placement or dispatch.

The KV cache eliminates attention computation for every new token, while routing assigns all following tokens to the same experts chosen during prefill. Network dispatch remains fixed, so expert-load imbalance cannot change serving latency.

The KV cache reuses prior attention keys and values, while the current token's hidden state is routed through selected feed-forward experts. Uneven expert demand, dispatch communication, and memory movement can still raise tail latency.

The KV cache stores previous token keys and values, but the MoE router must send each token through every expert to refresh cached states. This dense expert work is required before sparse routing resumes.
questions.explanation: Explanation: During autoregressive decoding, self-attention can reuse previous tokens' keys and values through a KV cache. That avoids recomputing those past projections, but a newly generated token still needs attention work and current-token expert routing. For example, a coding assistant might route successive generated tokens to different feed-forward experts. If many requests target the same remote expert, queues or all-to-all dispatch can increase p95 latency. The KV cache is not a cache of all experts' future results.

questions.stem: How should engineers distribute, monitor, and evaluate an MoE Transformer in production when experts span multiple GPUs and request patterns change?
options: Place experts across GPU groups and dispatch tokens by router scores, but compare deployments only by total parameter count. Sparse activation makes communication and p95 latency predictable without checking actual simultaneous traffic patterns or hardware.

Place expert weights across appropriate GPU groups, dispatch each token to its selected experts, and combine returned results. Monitor expert balance, token traffic, memory, throughput, p95 latency, task quality, and checkpoint recovery on real workloads.

Place experts across GPUs and track only aggregate average latency, but assign the same expert subset to every token to eliminate dynamic routing. This preserves learned specialization and removes the need to monitor expert-load imbalance.

Place expert weights on multiple GPUs and monitor utilization, but execute all remote experts for each token before weighting outputs. This guarantees sparse routing behavior while reliably avoiding all-to-all communication and checkpoint restoration testing entirely.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Serving an MoE Transformer may require expert parallelism, where different GPUs hold different expert weights. Selected token representations are dispatched to those devices and their outputs returned. For example, a multi-user assistant can slow down if many simultaneous requests select experts on one overloaded GPU. Track per-expert token counts, GPU memory, communication time, throughput, p95 latency, and answer quality. Compare active and total parameter counts, test realistic traffic shifts, and verify checkpoint restoration before rolling out new model versions.
